summary: Defines terminology for benchmarking resource reservation signaling in IntServ routers. These terms are meant to be used by later documents that define benchmarking methodologies or reporting formats. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before you can compare how fast different routers are at booking reserved lanes, you need agreed words for the measurements. This note makes that word list.

questions: what is benchmarking terminology for resource reservation routers
how to measure qos router performance
what are load factors in router benchmarking
subtitle: Standard vocabulary for measuring how well routers handle QoS reservation signaling.

tldr.problem: Vendors and network operators want to measure how well routers handle Quality of Service reservation protocols like RSVP, but lack standardized terminology, making it hard to compare products fairly.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines terms for benchmarking resource reservation routers: traffic flow types, load factors, performance metrics, and operational conditions. It allows vendors to measure and report signaling performance consistently.
tldr.outcome: Operators can now compare router products objectively, understand scalability limits, and plan network capacity for dynamic QoS provisioning.

today: RFC 4883 is Informational and defines benchmarking terminology. While RSVP and IntServ-based QoS have limited deployment in the modern Internet (differing approaches to QoS became more prevalent), this terminology remains useful for vendors and operators who do implement reservation-based QoS. The document provides the foundational language for any future benchmarking methodologies in this space.

sections.title: Benchmarking Quality of Service Signaling
sections.content:
Many networks want to offer Quality of Service (QoS) guarantees using the IntServ model, which requires routers to understand and respect resource reservations. The protocol most commonly used for this is RSVP (Resource ReSerVation Protocol). Before deploying RSVP on a network, operators need to understand a router's performance characteristics and scalability limits under various loads.

However, vendors had no standardized way to measure or report how well their routers handle QoS signaling. Without consistent terminology, one vendor might report signaling speed in one unit and another in different units, making comparisons impossible. This RFC solves that problem by defining a complete benchmarking vocabulary.

The terminology is designed to be protocol-independent (not tied to RSVP alone) while being grounded in real protocols like RSVP, NSIS, and others. The terms allow operators to measure how many QoS sessions a router can handle, how fast signaling messages are processed, and how signaling overhead affects data forwarding performance.
sections.eli5: Imagine buying routers and wanting to know: Can it handle 100 simultaneous QoS reservations? How long does a reservation request take? Will processing reservation requests slow down regular data traffic? This RFC provides the vocabulary to ask and answer these questions clearly.

sections.title: Traffic Types and Load Factors
sections.content:
The RFC defines several traffic flow types. A data flow is a stream of packets from one sender to multiple receivers, identified by a 5-tuple (source and destination IP addresses, ports, and protocol). A distinguished data flow receives special treatment by the router according to a QoS agreement, often getting higher priority. A best-effort data flow is traffic the router forwards without special handling, the default for most Internet traffic today.

The RFC then defines load factors that create measurable load on a router: the best-effort traffic load factor (number and size of best-effort packets per second), distinguished traffic load factor (number and size of QoS packets per second), session load factor (number of active QoS sessions), signaling intensity load factor (signaling messages per second), and signaling burst load factor (back-to-back signaling messages on one interface). Each load factor affects different router components differently.

A QoS session is an end-to-end relationship in which nodes agree on QoS treatment for specific data flows. The RFC emphasizes that routers must maintain reservation states for these sessions and process signaling messages that create, refresh, or tear down reservations. Soft-state protocols (like RSVP) require periodic refresh messages, while hard-state protocols require explicit teardown.
sections.eli5: There are different kinds of traffic: normal traffic, traffic that needs special handling, and signaling messages that set up the special handling. Each kind of traffic loads the router differently. The RFC is a way to count and control each kind.

sections.title: Measuring Router Performance
sections.content:
The RFC defines performance metrics for measuring router behavior. Signaling message handling time is the latency (delay) of a signaling message passing through the router. This affects how quickly QoS reservations are established, a critical metric for real-time applications. Distinguished traffic delay is the latency of a QoS packet passing through the router, including time for classification. Best-effort traffic delay is latency for normal packets, which indicates how much the signaling workload affects data forwarding.

Two metrics measure packet loss. Signaling message deficit is the ratio of lost signaling messages to expected messages (as a fraction from zero to one). This indicates whether a router can keep up with the signaling load. Session maintenance capacity (for soft-state protocols only) is the ratio of sessions actually being maintained to sessions that should be maintained, showing whether a router can refresh all active reservations when overloaded.

The RFC emphasizes that message handling time depends on message type: setting up a reservation typically takes longer than tearing one down. Similarly, the first message in a burst may be processed differently than subsequent identical messages. These variations must be documented.
sections.eli5: The measurements are: How fast do signaling messages go through the router? How fast do QoS packets go? How much slower do normal packets go? How many signaling messages get dropped? Can the router keep all QoS sessions alive?

sections.title: Operating Conditions and Scalability
sections.content:
A router can be in one of four conditions at any time, based on its ability to meet requirements. Loss-free and QoS compliant means the router forwards packets without loss, meets QoS guarantees, and processes signaling in timely fashion. Lossy but QoS compliant means some packets are dropped (from anywhere or only from QoS flows exceeding their allocation) but QoS requirements for privileged traffic are still met. Loss-free but not QoS compliant means all packets arrive but QoS guarantees are violated (e.g., latency too high). Neither loss-free nor QoS compliant means packets are lost and QoS is not met.

The scalability limit is the point where the router is still loss-free and QoS compliant but cannot handle additional load without entering a degraded condition. Finding scalability limits is the main goal of benchmarking: determining how many sessions, how much signaling intensity, or how much traffic the router can handle while still meeting its promises.

The RFC acknowledges that benchmarking happens in a black-box mode: testers cannot see the router's internal state, only external load and observable performance. Random early dropping for congestion control, for example, appears as packet loss but is a feature, not a failure. The definitions account for this by focusing on observable behavior and protocol compliance.
sections.eli5: A router is healthy as long as it doesn't drop packets and meets QoS promises. When you overload it, it will eventually start dropping packets or fail to deliver QoS. The scalability limit is where you find it tipping from healthy to struggling.

sections.title: Using the Terminology in Benchmarks
sections.content:
This RFC is a terminology document, not a methodology. It defines what to measure but not how. Future RFCs use these terms to specify benchmarking procedures. For example, a methodology RFC might say: 'Measure signaling message handling time with the session load factor at 1000 QoS sessions and the best-effort traffic load factor at [1000 pps; 64 bytes].'

The benefits of standard terminology are significant. Vendors can report results clearly and comparably. Operators can make purchase decisions based on published benchmarks. Network planners can use the measurements to size networks: if a router can maintain 500 sessions at a certain signaling rate, a network designer can estimate how much router capacity is needed for an expected number of reservations.

The RFC is based on analysis of multiple reservation protocols (RSVP, NSIS, YESSIR, ST2, and others) and builds on existing benchmarking work (RFC 1242 for network devices generally, RFC 2285 for LAN switching). It provides a foundation for vendors and operators to make objective, quantitative claims about router performance under QoS signaling load.
sections.eli5: Once everyone agrees on these terms, vendors can publish: 'Our router handles 1000 QoS sessions with an average signaling latency of 10 milliseconds.' Then everyone understands what that means and can compare it fairly to other routers.
